{{Short description|American physicist}}
'''Myron Lindsay (Bud) Good''' (October 25, 1923 – February 26, 1999) was an American physicist, a professor of physics at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] and [[Stony Brook University]].<ref name="pt99">{{citation|first1=Paul D.|last1=Grannis|first2=Janos|last2=Kirz|first3=Michael D.|last3=Marx|first4=Robert L.|last4=McCarthy|title=Myron Lindsay Good|journal=[[Physics Today]]|volume=52|issue=11|year=1999|doi=10.1063/1.882735|pages=75–76|bibcode = 1999PhT....52k..75G |s2cid=177897122 |doi-access=free}}.</ref><ref name="wisc">{{citation|title=Myron L. Good, 1923–1999|date=1999–2000|url=http://www.physics.wisc.edu/alumni/pdf/news99.pdf|journal=The Wisconsin Physicist|volume=6|issue=1|page=8}}.</ref><ref>[http://felix.physics.sunysb.edu/PAhist/mgood.html Myron L. Good] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100723220634/http://felix.physics.sunysb.edu/PAhist/mgood.html |date=2010-07-23 }}, Stony Brook University Physics Department, retrieved 2010-12-04.</ref>

Good's research interests spanned a broad range of topics in [[particle physics]]. He did important work on [[muon-catalyzed fusion]], [[Kaon]] regeneration, [[Hyperon|strange particles]], [[diffraction]] of particle beams, [[W and Z bosons|W boson]] [[Phenomenology (particle physics)|phenomenology]], and [[particle accelerator]] technology. Outside of particle physics, he also developed a theory of [[pulsar]]s as rotating [[neutron star]]s.<ref name="pt99"/>

Good did undergraduate studies at the [[University at Buffalo]] and [[Cornell University]], and received his Ph.D. in 1951 from [[Duke University]] for research on [[beta decay]]. His Ph.D. thesis was supervised by [[Henry W. Newson]].<ref name=PhysicsTree>{{cite web|title=Myron Lindsay Good|website=Physics Tree|url=https://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=52543}}</ref> After working as a research scientist at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], Good became a faculty member at the University of Wisconsin in 1959, and moved to Stony Brook in 1967. At Stony Brook, he headed the experimental particle physics group; he retired in 1992.<ref name="pt99"/>

He was elected in 1963 a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1963&unit_id=&institution=Madison%2C+Wisconsin}} (search on year=1963 and institution=Madison, Wisconsin)</ref> His doctoral students include [[Thomas Binford]] and [[Stanley Wojcicki]].<ref name=PhysicsTree/>
